findings.passage: A counterphobic Type 6 is the live alternative; Three, Two, Eight, Nine and Seven explain pieces.
findings.problem: The alternative that the title, description, 60-word answer and FAQ 2 all hinge on is labeled with a technical term the article never defines. Type 4 gets a plain-language sentence ("Type 4 is organized around identity..."); Type 6 never does. Its traits arrive piecemeal ("the shape Six theory predicts", "A Six's injury usually fuses fear and grievance", "Six theory predicts fear managed through preparation, allies and authority"), and the nearest gloss of "counterphobic" ("Counterphobic Sixes also charge at fear") lands roughly 2,500 words in, after the word has been used three times. No published 9takes people page uses "counterphobic", so a reader cannot lean on site familiarity either. "the Four's neighbor among the image types" is the same problem on a smaller scale.
findings.acceptance_test: By the end of the "What is Dakota Johnson's personality type?" section, a reader who has never heard of the Enneagram can say in one sentence what a Type 6 wants (certainty and support against a world that feels unsafe) and what "counterphobic" means (a Six who meets fear by charging at it instead of seeking cover), without following a link. Either add that sentence directly after the 60-word answer alongside the Type 4 sentence, or drop "counterphobic" from the 60-word answer and FAQ 1 and define it at "Read literally, that reflex is counterphobic." Gloss or cut "image types."

findings.passage: Yet in a decade of interviews about the films that went wrong, she has never described a set as a place where she was misled or left unprotected.
findings.problem: This is the sentence the whole profile rests on, and an unfamiliar reader meets two quotes that sound like exactly what it denies: the hook's "That is not what I thought we were making" two paragraphs earlier, and "I signed up to do a very different version of the film we ended up making" leading the Fifty Shades section. To someone with no prior knowledge, both read as complaints about being misled about what she agreed to. The article's answer exists (she was in the fight every day rather than discovering a betrayal, she assigns the gap to James's creative control, she says "both Jamie and I were treated really well" and James "was always kind to me"), but it is spread across the "Fear on one side" section and the limits paragraph some 1,500 words later and is never attached to those two quotes where they appear. The reader is asked to accept the thesis-defining distinction on trust at the exact moment the evidence seems to cut against it.
findings.acceptance_test: Where "signed up to do a very different version" first appears, one or two sentences name the objection ("that can sound like being misled") and answer it from the record: she describes being inside the fight daily ("It was always a battle", rewriting scenes the night before) rather than discovering a deception, locates the cause in creative control, and praises how she was treated. The intro's "never" either keeps that support within the same paragraph or is rewritten to state what she does say (where she locates the cause) rather than what she has never said. A first-time reader should be able to restate why "not the movie she signed up to make" differs from "misled" before reaching the "Fear on one side" section.

findings.passage: Of the Easter Bunny, she said in 2022, "Maybe that's why I make movies and why I want to make movies forever and ever. It makes things feel a little bit more safe."
findings.problem: The reader is never told the setup: she was recalling learning at 10 that the Easter Bunny was not real and said she would still believe in it if she could. Without it, "Of the Easter Bunny, she said" reads as a non sequitur, and the later callback ("The Easter Bunny line puts safety at the end of the sentence and moviemaking in its service") depends on a line the reader did not understand the first time. The evidence record (C98) already holds the setup wording.
findings.acceptance_test: One clause before the quote supplies the context from C98 (learning at 10 that the Easter Bunny did not exist; "if I could, I would still believe in it now") so that a reader who has not seen the Vanity Fair piece understands why movies and safety follow from the Easter Bunny.

findings.passage: On _The Lost Daughter_, she said in 2021, Maggie Gyllenhaal "kind of was my shepherd in that way.
findings.problem: Three names carry evidentiary weight through a relationship the article never states. Gyllenhaal is not identified as the film's director, so "shepherd" and "she knows what it feels like to not be seen" lose their meaning (an actress turned first-time director guiding her). Vanessa Burghardt is introduced only as a co-writer, not as the young actress who played her daughter in Cha Cha Real Smooth, so "with her, I feel very protective" has no referent. Alice Rohrwacher gets no descriptor, and the later "small Italian film" asks the reader to infer it from "Stromboli and Rome." The article already does this well elsewhere ("the former Netflix development executive Ro Donnelly", "the writer-director Cooper Raiff").
findings.acceptance_test: Each of Gyllenhaal, Burghardt and Rohrwacher carries a role descriptor at first mention, sourced to the existing evidence record (S03, S45, S01), so a reader can follow why the relationship matters without outside knowledge.

findings.passage: If one does, its shape will matter: a fight framed as being misled or left unprotected would point toward Six, one framed as the work made false toward Four.
findings.problem: The misled-or-unprotected versus work-made-false formulation appears in the intro, in the 60-word answer (paraphrased), at the top of "Fear on one side" ("the authority who misled her or left her exposed"), here, and again in FAQ 2. By this fourth body occurrence the reader is being told the test rather than shown anything new, and the body sits at 4,297 words against a 3,500-word target. One restatement helps an unfamiliar reader; four reads as a loop.
findings.acceptance_test: The full misled/unprotected versus work-made-false formulation appears at most twice in the body (once in the orientation, once in the "Fear on one side" test). This passage points forward in different words, for example by naming what a critical producer account would have to contain, and the trim is taken from restatement rather than from evidence.

findings.passage: Dakota Johnson Enneagram Type: Why 4 Leads a Live 6
findings.problem: The meta title is the first thing a searcher reads, and "Why 4 Leads a Live 6" is insider shorthand that reads like a score line to anyone who has not yet read the article. The description's closing "with Type 6 live" has the same problem. Both surfaces should orient a stranger, not reward someone who already knows the argument.
findings.acceptance_test: The meta title (35 to 65 characters) and the description (120 to 170 characters) state the result in words a first-time searcher can parse, for example "Dakota Johnson Enneagram Type: Type 4, With Type 6 Close Behind" and "...Why Type 4 leads and Type 6 stays close." A reader shown only the meta title can say which type the article argues for and that a second type is seriously in play.

findings.passage: the only child the actors Don Johnson and Melanie Griffith had together and one of seven half-siblings
findings.problem: A reader cannot tell whether she has seven half-siblings or is one of seven children. The phrasing follows Vanity Fair's own ambiguous line ("She is one of seven half siblings", S02), so the draft is faithful to its source but inherits the confusion, and the article asserts it in its own voice.
findings.acceptance_test: Rephrase to what the source supports without asserting a count it leaves ambiguous (for example, "with half-siblings on both sides of a large blended family"), or attribute the count to Vanity Fair in its own words. A reader should not be left computing family size.

protected_passages.passage: "I found myself as an actor, a few times, showing up to the premiere of a movie to see it the first time," she said. Her verdict on those nights: "That is not what I thought we were making."
protected_passages.reason: A sourced, dated, specific opening that a stranger understands instantly and that poses the exact question the article answers. Do not replace it with a fear quote or a biographical lead.

protected_passages.passage: Not that she was good, or that she had arrived. That she did something different.
protected_passages.reason: Turns a biographical detail (the Fincher compliment) into the first piece of the argument in two short sentences, teaching the reader how to read the rest of the quotes.

protected_passages.passage: Her fullest telling also has fear in it, and where the fear sits matters.
protected_passages.reason: The move that makes the Four-versus-Six case honest for a newcomer: the strongest Six evidence is quoted inside the thesis-bearing passage rather than parked in a caveat section, and the sentence tells the reader what to watch for.

protected_passages.passage: A Seven's appetite usually runs from that sentence. Hers runs toward it.
protected_passages.reason: The alternatives section could have been a checklist; this is a verified quote turned into a discriminating observation in nine words. Keep the rhythm of the other type paragraphs that end on a turn like this.

protected_passages.passage: What she keeps losing, and keeps going back to build, is the connection inside it.
protected_passages.reason: The ending lands on the 2026 wrap-grief quote without a CTA or a thesis recap, and it still works if the Verity release detail is removed. It is the five-year sentence.

assessment: Read cold, this orients fast: the first sentence says who she is and the hook poses the question in her own words. A stranger leaves knowing the Fifty Shades creative-control fight (with the 2017 director corroboration and the author's 2015 side), why TeaTime exists, what the Ellen clip and the limes were, and how fear and grievance are being distinguished. Momentum is strong through "Fear on one side, grievance on the other," which pays off the setup; after "Hence medium confidence" the piece becomes a tour (persona, five other types, open items) for about 1,300 words before the strong ending, which is acceptable because each section does required work, but it is where the 4,297-word body could lose 400 to 600 words. The two majors are clarity problems at the spine: Type 6 and "counterphobic" are never defined for a reader who does not already know the system, and the thesis-defining distinction between "the work was made into something else" and "I was misled" is asserted in the intro and only defended 1,500 words later, while an unfamiliar reader hears "signed up to do a very different version" as the very thing being denied. Fix those two and the profile is readable by someone who has never opened an Enneagram page. Similarity: all three tripped pairs (0.531, 0.216, 0.186) are self-matches against the earlier 2026-10-07 Dakota Johnson draft of the same subject; the highest cross-subject score is 0.053 (jeremy-allen-white) with no shared phrases and a different argument, so there is no meaningful reuse to report. Not an open case (profile_format standard); eligibility rules do not apply. Risks carried forward: the Fifty Shades account concerns a named living person who has not responded, and the typing is contested at medium confidence.
